arXiv:1601.02066v1 [math.DG] 09 Jan 2016

Three circles theorems for harmonic functions

Guoyi Xu Address: Yau Mathematical Sciences Center
Jin Chun Yuan West Building
Tsinghua University, Beijing
P. R. China, 100084 Email address: gyxu@math.tsinghua.edu.cn
Abstract.

We proved two Three Circles Theorems for harmonic functions on manifolds in integral sense. As one application, on manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature, whose tangent cone at infinity is the unique metric cone with unique conic measure, we showed the existence of nonconstant harmonic functions with polynomial growth. This existence result recovered and generalized the former result of Y. Ding, and led to a complete answer of L. Ni’s conjecture. Furthermore in similar context, combining the techniques of estimating the frequency of harmonic functions with polynomial growth, which were developed by Colding and Minicozzi, we confirmed their conjecture about the uniform bound of frequency.

Key words and phrases: 
harmonic function, existence, frequency

35B40, 58J05, 53C23, 35A01

1. Introduction

In 19751975, S.-T. Yau [47] generalized the classical Liouville theorem to complete manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature. Specially, he proved that any positive harmonic function on such manifolds is constant. In [11], S.-Y. Cheng further proved that on such manifolds any harmonic function of sublinear growth must be constant. On complete manifolds, harmonic functions with polynomial growth are important analytic functions besides the Green’s function and the heat kernel (note the latter two have singularities).

In the study of harmonic functions on complete manifolds, Yau considered the space of harmonic functions with polynomial growth:

ℋd(M)={u|u(x)isharmoniconMn;|u(x)|≤K(ρ(x)+1)dforsomeK>0}\displaystyle\mathscr{H}_{d}(M)=\{u|\ u(x)\ is\ harmonic\ on\ M^{n}\ ;|u(x)|\leq K(\rho(x)+1)^{d}\ for\ some\ K>0\}

where ρ⁡(x)=d⁡(p,x)\rho(x)=d(p,x) and pp is some fixed point on MnM^{n}. In [48], the following conjecture was made:

Conjecture 1.1 (S.-T. Yau).

Let MnM^{n} be a complete manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature, then d​i​m​(ℋd​(M))<∞dim\big(\mathscr{H}_{d}(M)\big)<\infty for any d>0d>0.

P. Li and L.-F. Tam firstly proved the conjecture for linear growth harmonic function (d=1d=1) in [31], and they further verified the 22-dimensional case (n=2n=2) in [32]. In 19971997, this conjecture was completely proved by Colding and Minicozzi [14] (also see [35], [17], [18] and [33] for further developments). Although Yau’s conjecture was confirmed, there are still several important questions about harmonic functions with polynomial growth remained open.

It is well known that on any complete noncompact manifold, there always exist nonconstant harmonic functions (see [25]). A natural question is about the existence of nonconstant harmonic function with polynomial growth. Note any complete manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature has at least linear volume growth (see [47]). C. Sormani proved the following:

Theorem 1.2 ([43]).

Let MnM^{n} be a complete manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature and at most linear volume growth. If there exists a nonconstant harmonic function of polynomial growth, then the manifold splits isometrically, Mn=ℝ×Nn−1M^{n}=\mathbb{R}\times N^{n-1}.

As observed in [22], there exists a suitable metric on ℝ+×𝕊n−1\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\mathbb{S}^{n-1}, which has nonnegative Ricci curvature and linear volume growth, but can not split isometrically. From Theorem 1.2, it will not admit any nonconstant harmonic functions with polynomial growth. A concrete example is given in Section 4 (Example 4.8).

Hence, to study the existence of nonconstant harmonic function with polynomial growth in nonnegative Ricci curvature context, we need to have some restriction on the volume growth of MnM^{n}. To the author’s knowledge, the following question is still open :

Question 1.3.

If (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete manifold with R​c≥0Rc\geq 0 and maximal volume growth, does there exist d≥1d\geq 1 such that d​i​m​(ℋd​(M))≥2dim\big(\mathscr{H}_{d}(M)\big)\geq 2? In other words, is there any nonconstant harmonic function with polynomial growth order at most dd on MnM^{n}?

In another direction, putting the existence problem in the positively curved context, L. Ni [39] made the following conjecture:

Conjecture 1.4 (L. Ni).

Let (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) be a complete Riemannian manifold of positive sectional curvature, the necessary and sufficient condition that MnM^{n} admits nonconstant harmonic functions of polynomial growth is, that MnM^{n} is of maximum volume growth.

For the corresponding conjecture on Kähler manifolds, L. Ni proved that if the manifold is complete Kähler with bounded nonnegative bisectional curvature and of maximum volume growth, it admits nonconstant holomorphic functions of polynomial growht (see Corollary 11 of [38]). On the other hand, recently, G. Liu (see Theorem 22 of [36]) showed that if MM is a complete noncompact Kähler manifold with positive bisectional curvature, and it admits a nonconstant holomorphic function with polynomial growth, then MM is of maximal volume growth.

In Riemannian geometry context, Y. Ding [22] proved that on complete manifolds with R​c≥0Rc\geq 0, maximal volume growth and the unique tangent cone at infinity, there exists nonconstant harmonic function with polynomial growth. Note when MnM^{n} has nonnegative sectional curvature, from Theorem I​.26I.26 in [12], the tangent cone at infinity of MnM^{n} is the unique metric cone C⁡(Y)C(Y), where YY is a compact metric space. Hence Ding’s existence result will imply the sufficient part of Conjecture 1.4. However we have some difficulties to verify the proof of Ding’s existence result. For example, Lemma 1.11.1, Corollary 1.111.11 and Lemma 1.21.2 in [22] does not hold for zero function.

The main technical tool in [22] is a generalization of the monotonicity of frequency for harmonic functions on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, which is a type of Three Circles Theorem in L2L^{2} sense on complete manifolds (also see [49] and [13] for related results).

The classical Hadamard’s Three Circles Theorem was implied in the announcement [27] published in 18961896, we state it as the following form, which is sort of consistent with our presentation in Theorem 3.2 and Theorem 3.4 of this paper.

Theorem 1.5 (Hadamard’s Three Circles Theorem).

If f⁡(z)f(z) is a holomorphic function on {z|r4≤|z|≤r}⊂ℂ\{z|\ \frac{r}{4}\leq|z|\leq r\}\subset\mathbb{C}, where r>0r>0 is some constant, then

(1.1) M⁡(r/2)M⁡(r/4)≤M⁡(r)M⁡(r/2)\displaystyle\frac{M(r/2)}{M(r/4)}\leq\frac{M(r)}{M(r/2)}

where M⁡(s):=max|z|=s⁡{|f⁡(z)|}M(s)\vcentcolon=\max_{|z|=s}\{|f(z)|\},

The classical Hadamard Three Circles Theorem for holomorphic functions had also been generalized to solutions of partial differential equations in different contexts by L. Simon [42], J. Cheeger and G. Tian [7], G. Liu [37]. In spite of our concerns about the argument in [22], partially motivated by the results there, we proved two modified Three Circles Theorems for harmonic functions in integral sense (see Theorem 3.2 and Theorem 3.4 in Section 3).

Remark 1.6.

One novel thing in one of our Three Circles theorems (Theorem 3.2) is that it can be applied for the collapsed case, i.e. the case that the maximal volume growth assumption does not hold. Also Theorem 3.2 is dealing with the integral JuJ_{u}, whose domain is different from the original one considered in [22] (see Corollary 1.111.11 there). View from the domains of the integral appearing in those results, Theorem 3.2 is more like a three disks theorem, and Ding’s technical tool is based on a three annuli theorem.

As one application of our Three Circles Theorems, we proved the following theorem, which generalizes the existence result in [22].

Theorem 1.7.

Let (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) be a complete manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature, the tangent cone at infinity with renormalized limit measure is a unique metric cone C⁡(X)C(X) with the unique conic measure of power κ≥2\kappa\geq 2, and ℋ1​(X)>0\mathcal{H}^{1}(X)>0. Then

(1.2) inf{α|α∈𝒟(M),α≠0}<∞\displaystyle\inf\{\alpha|\ \alpha\in\mathscr{D}(M),\alpha\neq 0\}<\infty

and for any d>inf{α|α∈𝒟(M),α≠0}d>\inf\{\alpha|\ \alpha\in\mathscr{D}(M),\alpha\neq 0\},

(1.3) d​i​m​(ℋd​(M))≥2\displaystyle dim\big(\mathscr{H}_{d}(M)\big)\geq 2

The conic measure of power κ\kappa and 𝒟⁡(M)\mathscr{D}(M) will be defined in Section 2.

Generally, we do not know the uniqueness of the renormalized limit measure with respect to one tangent cone at infinity of the manifold (compare Example 1.241.24 of [4]). However, from Theorem 5.95.9 of [4], if (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete manifold with R​c≥0Rc\geq 0 and maximal volume growth, then every tangent cone at infinity has its unique renormalized measure; and the measure is a multiple of Hausdorff measure ℋn\mathcal{H}^{n}, which is a conic measure of power nn. Hence, Theorem 1.7 implies the existence result in [22] mentioned above. The uniqueness of tangent cone at infinity is an important and hard problem, which was addressed in [7] and [20] for Ricci flat manifolds under various assumptions.

Remark 1.8.

When (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete manifold with R​c≥0Rc\geq 0 and maximal volume growth, S. Honda [28] showed d​i​m​(ℋd​(M))=1dim\big(\mathscr{H}_{d}(M)\big)=1 for any d<inf{α|α∈𝒟(M),α≠0}d<\inf\{\alpha|\ \alpha\in\mathscr{D}(M),\alpha\neq 0\}. Hence the conclusion of Theorem 1.7 seems to be a sharp result except that the critical case d=inf{α|α∈𝒟(M),α≠0}d=\inf\{\alpha|\ \alpha\in\mathscr{D}(M),\alpha\neq 0\} is not clear yet.

To prove Theorem 1.7, we partially followed the strategy in [22]. Because our Three Circles Theorem (Theorem 3.2) works for the collapsed case too, we succeeded in proving the existence of nonconstant harmonic functions with polynomial growth in the collapsed case first time, although with additional assumptions.

More concretely, to construct one nonconstant harmonic function with polynomial growth, we firstly choose a suitable harmonic function of polynomial growth on the tangent cone at infinity of the manifold, where we used the assumptions that the manifold has the conic renormalized limit measure and the tangent cone at infinity is a metric cone.

Then we use the results of Cheeger [9], to get a sequence of approximate functions defined on a sequence of increasing geodesic balls exhausting the manifold, which are vanishing at the same fixed point. Solving the Dirichlet problem on those geodesic balls with the same boundary conditions as the corresponding approximate functions, this yields a family of harmonic functions defined on the exhausting domains of the manifold.

Because the sequence of harmonic functions constructed as above have the asymptotic growth behavior as the chosen harmonic function of polynomial growth on the tangent cone at infinity, we can get that the the ratio between the average integrals of those harmonic functions on bigger domain and smaller domain are uniformly bounded near infinity, where the bound depends on the growth rate of the harmonic function of polynomial growth on the tangent cone at infinity chosen above.

If we can get ‘some induction estimate’ of the ratios from outer domains to inner domains, the uniform polynomial bound of the family of harmonic functions will be obtained by the induction method. Then, after the suitable rescaling, using the well-known Cheng-Yau’s gradient estimate for harmonic functions in [10], combining with the Arzela-Ascoli theorem, for some subsequence of these harmonic functions, we get the limit function defined on the whole manifold, which is harmonic function of polynomial growth. The nonconstancy of the limit function follows from its vanishing at the fixed point, and the non-vanishing of some local integral of the limit function, which resulted from the suitable chosen rescaling mentioned above.

Our Three Circles Theorem (Theorem 3.2) will play the role of the ‘induction estimate’ needed in the above argument. Starting from the eigenfunctions expansion of harmonic functions on the metric cone with conic measure, the key idea to prove the Three Circles Theorem, is to use the gap between the eigenvalues of the tangent cone’s cross-section. When the tangent cone at infinity with renormalized limit measure is the unique metric cone with unique conic measure, this gap is implied by the discreteness of the spectrum of Laplace operator on the cross-section, and we get the last piece in the proof of Theorem 1.7.

When nonconstant harmonic functions with polynomial growth exist on complete manifolds, as proved in [15], the bound of frequency is essential to describe the asymptotic structure of those functions (like the almost separation of variables). Hence a natural question is about the uniform bound of frequency of harmonic functions on manifolds. Based on the study in [15], Colding and Minicozzi posed the following conjecture:

Conjecture 1.9 ([16]).

Suppose that MnM^{n} has nonnegative Ricci curvature and maximal volume growth. If u∈ℋd​(M)u\in\mathscr{H}_{d}(M) for some d>0d>0, then the frequency of uu is uniformly bounded.

Remark 1.10.

Besides [15] and [16], the frequency was also studied in [1] and [23]. For more related reference about the frequency, the reader can consult Remark 2.162.16 in [15]. We would like to point out that the monotonicity of the frequency in Euclidean space can be viewed as the quantitative version of the classical Three Circles Theorem.

Roughly say, to get the uniform bound of the frequency, we only need to control the ratios of I⁡(r)I(r) on concentric circles with increasing radii. Checking the results and techniques developed in [15] carefully, the ratios have uniform bound on a sequence of concentric circles, whose radii are approaching the infinity. If a suitable Three Circles Theorem is available, the uniform bound of ratios can be obtained by the induction method similar as the former argument, which will imply the uniform bound of the frequency. Hence, using the Three Circles Theorem (Theorem 3.4) established in Section 3, we proved the following theorem:

Theorem 1.11.

Suppose that (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has nonnegative Ricci curvature and maximal volume growth, also assume the tangent cone at infinity of MnM^{n} is unique. Then for u​(x)∈ℋd​(M)u(x)\in\mathscr{H}_{d}(M), the frequency of u⁡(x)u(x) is uniformly bounded by C⁡(u,n,VM,d)C(u,n,V_{M},d).

Remark 1.12.

This theorem confirms Conjecture 1.9 with the additional assumption the uniqueness of the tangent cone at infinity of manifolds. In fact, we proved a stronger result which implies Theorem 1.11, see Theorem 5.5 in Section 5 for details.

As we mentioned before, from [12], for any complete manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature, the tangent cone at infinity is a unique metric cone. From Theorem 1.7, we have the following corollary.

Corollary 1.13.

Suppose that (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has nonnegative sectional curvature, the tangent cone at infinity with renormalized limit measure is a unique metric cone C⁡(X)C(X) with the unique conic measure of power κ≥2\kappa\geq 2, and ℋ1​(X)>0\mathcal{H}^{1}(X)>0. Then (1.2) and (1.3) hold.

Remark 1.14.

On non-negatively curved manifolds, maximal volume growth implies the uniqueness of the tangent cone at infinity and the conic renormalized limit measure of power κ=n\kappa=n and ℋn−1​(X)>0\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(X)>0, hence the sufficient part of Conjecture 1.4 is implied by Corollary 1.13.

On the other hand, there exists complete manifolds MnM^{n} with positive sectional curvature, whose tangent cone at infinity C⁡(X)C(X) has the unique renormalized limit measure, which is conic measure of power κ≥2\kappa\geq 2 and ℋ1​(X)>0\mathcal{H}^{1}(X)>0 (see Example 4.9). Hence by Corollary 1.13, Example 4.9 is a counterexample to the necessary part of Conjecture 1.4.

The organization of this paper is as the following. In Section 2, we stated some background facts about Gromov-Hausdorff convergence and Cheeger-Colding’s theory, which are needed for later sections. We also recalled the definition of frequency function and the related formulas.

In Section 3, we proved two Three Circles Theorems, which are the key technical tools applicable for the existence and frequency problems respectively. For both theorems, the method is proof by contradiction and reduced the related analysis to the analysis on the tangent cone at infinity.

In Section 4, we constructed the nonconstant harmonic function of polynomial growth from the harmonic function on the tangent cones at infinity. And the Three Circles Theorem is used to guarantee the polynomial growth of the constructed harmonic function. We also constructed two example manifolds, which address the nonexistence and existence of harmonic functions with polynomial growth, under linear volume growth and at least quadratic volume growth assumptions respectively. Specially, one example is the first counterexample to the necessary part of Conjecture 1.4.

In Section 5, using the other Three Circles Theorem, combining the results and techniques developed in [15], we proved the uniform bound of frequency. Some technical results in this section are well-known from [15] in more general context, but we provide the details here to make our argument self-contained in this concrete case.

2. Background and notations

In this section, we always assume that (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is an nn-dimensional complete manifold with R​c≥0Rc\geq 0. We firstly review some background material about Gromov-Hausdorff convergence and analysis on limit spaces.

Let {(Min,pi,ρi)}\big\{(M_{i}^{n},p_{i},\rho_{i})\big\} be a sequence of pointed Riemannian manifolds, where pi∈Minp_{i}\in M_{i}^{n} and ρi\rho_{i} is the metric on MinM_{i}^{n}. If {(Min,pi,ρi)}\big\{(M_{i}^{n},p_{i},\rho_{i})\big\} converges to (M∞,p∞,ρ∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty}) in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense, we write (Min,pi,ρi)⟶dG​H(M∞,p∞,ρ∞)\displaystyle(M_{i}^{n},p_{i},\rho_{i})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d_{GH}}}{{\longrightarrow}}(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty}). See [26] for the definition and basic facts concerning Gromov-Hausdorff convergence.

A metric space (M∞,p∞,ρ∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty}) is a tangent cone at infinity of MnM^{n} if it is a Gromov-Hausdorff limit of a sequence of rescaled manifolds (Mn,p,rj−2​g)(M^{n},p,r_{j}^{-2}g), where rj→∞r_{j}\rightarrow\infty. By Gromov’s compactness theorem, [26], any sequence rj→∞r_{j}\rightarrow\infty, has a subsequence, also denoted as rj→∞r_{j}\rightarrow\infty, such that the rescaled manifolds (Mn,p,rj−2​g)(M^{n},p,r_{j}^{-2}g) converge to some tangent cone at infinity M∞M_{\infty} in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense.

Let us recall that from Bishop-Gromov’s volume comparison theorem, we can define the asymptotic volume ratio

(2.1) VM=limr→∞V⁡(r)rn\displaystyle V_{M}=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}\frac{V(r)}{r^{n}}

where V⁡(r)V(r) is the volume of the geodesic ball B⁡(r)B(r) centered at pp with radius rr. And the above definition is independent of pp, so we omit pp there. If VM>0V_{M}>0, we say that (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has maximal volume growth. Note VM≤V0n​(1)V_{M}\leq V_{0}^{n}(1) from Bishop-Gromov’s volume comparison theorem, where Vkn​(r)V_{k}^{n}(r) is the volume of ball with radius rr in the nn-dimensional space form with sectional curvature equal to kk.

Example of Perelman [40] shows that tangent cone at infinity is not unique in general even if the manifold with R​c≥0Rc\geq 0 has maximal volume growth and quadratic curvature decay. Although the tangent cone at infinity may be not unique, under maximal volume growth assumption, Cheeger and Colding proved the following theorem characterizing it:

Theorem 2.1 ([3]).

Let MnM^{n} be a complete manifold with R​c≥0Rc\geq 0 and maximal volume growth, then every tangent cone at infinity M∞M_{\infty} is a metric cone C⁡(X)C(X), where XX is a compact metric space and d​i​a​m​(X)≤πdiam(X)\leq\pi.

Note the metric on the metric cone C⁡(X)C(X) is d​r2+r2​d​Xdr^{2}+r^{2}dX, where r∈[0,∞)r\in[0,\infty).

In the collapsed case (i.e. the maximal volume growth assumption does not hold), we can consider the renormalized measure on the limit space under the measured Gromov-Hausdorff convergence. As in Section 99 of [9], we have the following definition.

Definition 2.2.

If ωi\omega_{i}, ω∞\omega_{\infty} are Borel regular measures on MinM_{i}^{n}, M∞M_{\infty}, we say that (Min,pi,ρi,ωi)(M_{i}^{n},p_{i},\rho_{i},\omega_{i}) converges to (M∞,p∞,ρ∞,ω∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty},\omega_{\infty}) in the measured Gromov-Hausdorff sense, if (Min,pi,ρi)⟶dG​H(M∞,p∞,ρ∞)(M_{i}^{n},p_{i},\rho_{i})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d_{GH}}}{{\longrightarrow}}(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty}), in addition, for any xi→x∞x_{i}\rightarrow x_{\infty}, (xi∈Minx_{i}\in M_{i}^{n}, x∞∈M∞x_{\infty}\in M_{\infty}), r>0r>0, we have

and

Definition 2.3.

On a metric cone (C⁡(X),d​r2+r2​d​X)(C(X),dr^{2}+r^{2}dX), ν\nu is called conic measure of power κ\kappa, and κ\kappa is a positive constant denoted as 𝚙⁡(ν)\mathtt{p}(\nu), if for any Ω⊂⊂C⁡(X)\Omega\subset\subset C(X),

(2.5) ν⁡(Ω)=∫0∞rκ−1​𝑑r​∫Xχ⁡(Ωr)​d​ν−1\displaystyle\nu(\Omega)=\int_{0}^{\infty}r^{\kappa-1}dr\int_{X}\chi(\Omega_{r})d\nu_{-1}

where Ωr={z|z∈Ω,r(z)=r}\Omega_{r}=\{z|z\in\Omega,r(z)=r\}, χ⁡(⋅)\chi(\cdot) is the characteristic function on C⁡(X)C(X).

If (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete manifold with R​c≥0Rc\geq 0 and maximal volume growth, from Theorem 2.1 above and Theorem 5.95.9 in [4], every tangent cone at infinity of MnM^{n} is a metric cone, with the unique corresponding renormalized limit measure, which is a conic measure of power nn. In collapsing case, our definition of conic measure will play the role of co-area formula on metric cones in non-collapsing case, which was showed in Section 77 of [28].

Assume that (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete manifold with R​c≥0Rc\geq 0, all tangent cones at infinity are metric cones and every renormalized limit measure is conic measure, we define the set of all tangent cones at infinity of MnM^{n} with renormalized limit measure as ℳ(M):={(C(X),ν)|C(X)\mathscr{M}(M)\vcentcolon=\{(C(X),\nu)|\ C(X) is the metric tangent cone at infinity of MnM^{n}, ν\nu is the conic renormalized limit measure}\}.

From [6] (also see [9]), there exists a self-adjoint Laplace operator Δ(C⁡(X),ν)\Delta_{(C(X),\nu)} on (C⁡(X),ν)∈ℳ⁡(M)(C(X),\nu)\in\mathscr{M}(M). From (2.3) and (2.4), ν\nu induces a natural measure ν−1\nu_{-1} on XX, which satisfies a volume doubling property. Similar argument as in [21] (see Section 44 there), weak Poincaré inequality also holds on (X,ν−1)(X,\nu_{-1}). Hence from [6] (also see [9]), volume doubling property, weak Poincaré inequality and the rectifiability of the cross section XX yields the existence of a self-adjoint positive Laplace operator Δ(X,ν−1)\Delta_{(X,\nu_{-1})} on (X,ν−1)(X,\nu_{-1}).

When ℋ1​(X)>0\mathcal{H}^{1}(X)>0 where ℋi\mathcal{H}^{i} is ii-dimensional Hausdorff measure, L2​(X)L^{2}(X) is an infinite dimensional Hilbert space. Now from Rellich-type Compactness Theorem (Theorem 4.94.9 of [29], also see the Appendix of [46]), similar as the standard elliptic theory on compact manifolds (see Chapter 66 in [45] etc.), on compact metric measure space (X,ν−1)(X,\nu_{-1}), we have an orthonormal basis {φi​(x)}i=1∞\{\varphi_{i}(x)\}_{i=1}^{\infty} for L2​(X)L^{2}(X), and a sequence 0=λ1<λ2≤λ3≤⋯0=\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}\leq\lambda_{3}\leq\cdots, limi→∞λi=∞\lim_{i\rightarrow\infty}\lambda_{i}=\infty, such that

(2.6) Δ(X,ν−1)​φi​(x)=−λi​φi​(x)\displaystyle\Delta_{(X,\nu_{-1})}\varphi_{i}(x)=-\lambda_{i}\varphi_{i}(x)

Now assume that (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete manifold with R​c≥0Rc\geq 0, all tangent cones at infinity are metric cones and every renormalized limit measure is conic measure, and ℋ1​(X)>0\mathcal{H}^{1}(X)>0. Then we have the following proposition:

For any (C⁡(X),ν)∈ℳ⁡(M)(C(X),\nu)\in\mathscr{M}(M), assume that conic measure ν\nu is of power κ>0\kappa>0, for any u⁡(x)∈H01​(C⁡(X))u(x)\in H_{0}^{1}(C(X)),

(2.7) Δ(C⁡(X),ν)​u=∂2u∂r2+κ−1r​∂u∂r+1r2​Δ(X,ν−1)​u\displaystyle\Delta_{(C(X),\nu)}u=\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial r^{2}}+\frac{\kappa-1}{r}\frac{\partial u}{\partial r}+\frac{1}{r^{2}}\Delta_{(X,\nu_{-1})}u

∫C⁡(X)Δ(C⁡(X),ν)u⋅wdν=−∫C⁡(X)∇u⋅∇wdν=−∫0∞rκ−1(∫X∇u⋅∇wdν−1)dr\displaystyle\int_{C(X)}\Delta_{(C(X),\nu)}u\cdot wd\nu=-\int_{C(X)}\nabla u\cdot\nabla wd\nu=-\int_{0}^{\infty}r^{\kappa-1}\Big(\int_{X}\nabla u\cdot\nabla wd\nu_{-1}\Big)dr
(2.8) =−∫0∞rκ−1(∫X(∇ru+1r∇xu)⋅(∇rw+1r∇xw)dν−1(x))dr\displaystyle\quad\quad=-\int_{0}^{\infty}r^{\kappa-1}\Big(\int_{X}(\nabla_{r}u+\frac{1}{r}\nabla_{x}u)\cdot(\nabla_{r}w+\frac{1}{r}\nabla_{x}w)d\nu_{-1}(x)\Big)dr
=−∫0∞rκ−3(∫X∇xu⋅∇xwdν−1(x))dr−∫0∞rκ−1∫X∇ru⋅∇rwdν−1(x)\displaystyle\quad\quad=-\int_{0}^{\infty}r^{\kappa-3}\Big(\int_{X}\nabla_{x}u\cdot\nabla_{x}wd\nu_{-1}(x)\Big)dr-\int_{0}^{\infty}r^{\kappa-1}\int_{X}\nabla_{r}u\cdot\nabla_{r}wd\nu_{-1}(x)
=∫0∞rκ−1​∫X1r2​Δ(X,ν−1)​u⋅w+∫0∞rκ−1​∫X(∂2u∂r2+κ−1r​∂u∂r)⋅w\displaystyle\quad\quad=\int_{0}^{\infty}r^{\kappa-1}\int_{X}\frac{1}{r^{2}}\Delta_{(X,\nu_{-1})}u\cdot w+\int_{0}^{\infty}r^{\kappa-1}\int_{X}\Big(\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial r^{2}}+\frac{\kappa-1}{r}\frac{\partial u}{\partial r}\Big)\cdot w

where (2.8) follows from the metric cone structure of C⁡(X)C(X).

From (2.9), we obtain (2.7). ∎

The following corollary is similar as Theorem 1.111.11 of [15] (also see [8]), for completeness we provide its proof here following the argument in [15].

If uu is a harmonic function on (C⁡(X),ν)(C(X),\nu) with respect to Δ(C⁡(X),ν)\Delta_{(C(X),\nu)}, then

3. Three Circles Theorems for harmonic functions

Different types of Three Circles Theorems were proved by Simon [42], Cheeger and Tian [7], Colding, DeLellis and Minicozzi [13] in different contexts. Also see Zhang [49], Ding [22] for harmonic functions on manifolds and Liu [37] for holomorphic functions on Kähler manifolds.

However, to study Question 1.3, Conjecture 1.4 and Conjecture 1.9, we need to do some modification to get the Three Circles Theorems applicable on those problems.

Lemma 3.1.

and (3.2) is equivalent to

Note

(3.5) ∑αi≠α12−2​αi​wi​(1−22​(α−αi))≤∑αi≠α12−2​α​wi​(1−22​(α−αi))\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha_{i}\neq\alpha_{1}}2^{-2\alpha_{i}}w_{i}(1-2^{2(\alpha-\alpha_{i})})\leq\sum_{\alpha_{i}\neq\alpha_{1}}2^{-2\alpha}w_{i}(1-2^{2(\alpha-\alpha_{i})})

5. Uniform bound of frequency function

Much of argument in this section followed the detailed analysis about frequency function in [15] (especially Proposition 3.33.3, Proposition 3.363.36, Proposition 4.114.11 and Lemma 7.17.1 there). Theorem 5.5.

Suppose that (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has nonnegative Ricci curvature and maximal volume growth. For u∈ℋd​(M)u\in\mathscr{H}_{d}(M), if 5​d∉𝒟⁡(M)5d\notin\mathscr{D}(M), then the frequency of uu is bounded by C⁡(u,n,VM,d)C(u,n,V_{M},d).

Proof: If uu has no zero point, then by Yau’s Liouville theorem [47] uu is constant, the conclusion is straightforward. Assume u⁡(p)=0u(p)=0 where p∈Mp\in M is some fixed point. We will firstly prove the following claim:

Now we prove Theorem 1.11 by using the above theorem.

Proof of Theorem 1.11:  If d<1d<1, from [11] uu must be constant, then the conclusion follows trivially. Hence we assume d≥1d\geq 1 in the rest of the proof. When the tangent cone at infinity of MnM^{n} is unique, denoted as C⁡(X)C(X), then 𝒟⁡(M)\mathscr{D}(M) is a countable set by the fact that the spectrum of C⁡(X)C(X) is discrete. Because d≥1d\geq 1, we can find d0∈[d,d+1]d_{0}\in[d,d+1] such that 5​d0∉𝒟⁡(M)5d_{0}\notin\mathscr{D}(M), note u∈ℋd​(M)⊂ℋd0​(M)u\in\mathscr{H}_{d}(M)\subset\mathscr{H}_{d_{0}}(M). From Theorem 5.5, ℱu​(r)≤C⁡(u,n,VM,d0)≤C⁡(u,n,VM,d)\mathscr{F}_{u}(r)\leq C(u,n,V_{M},d_{0})\leq C(u,n,V_{M},d), the conclusion is proved. ∎
